title: Braaied Snoek with Apricot Glaze
author: Oom Danie
desc: A whole snoek butterflied open and dried, braaied skin side down for four fifths of the cook, basted with apricot jam melted into butter, garlic and lemon whenever the flesh is facing up.
longDesc: Snoek over coals with an apricot and garlic glaze is a Western Cape institution, and the sequence matters more than the glaze does. The fish goes on skin side down and stays there for about eighty per cent of a fifteen-minute cook, because the skin protects the flesh from the coals and the glaze needs a flesh-side-up window to be basted into. Drying the fish first is the most West Coast detail in the whole recipe: hang it in a draught if you happen to live in a fishing village, and blot it with paper towel if you do not.
ingredients: 1 whole snoek, cleaned, head and tail removed, butterflied open
Salt and freshly ground black pepper
steps: Dry the butterflied snoek: hang it in a draught, salt it with coarse sea salt, or blot it well with paper towel.
Lightly fry the chopped garlic in the butter in a small saucepan.
Add the apricot jam and the lemon juice, along with the soy sauce, wine or chilli sauce if you are using them.
Heat and stir until everything has melted and combined.
Lay the fish open in a hinged grid and put it on over medium coals, skin side down. Season the flesh with salt and pepper once it is on the grid.
Baste the flesh generously with the glaze while it is facing up.
With foil under the skin: 10 minutes skin side down, then 3 minutes flesh side down with the foil removed, then a final 2 minutes skin side down to brown the skin.
Directly on the grid with no foil: about 12 minutes skin side down, then 3 minutes flesh side down to brown.
Test it by pushing a fork into the thickest part and turning it slightly. If the flesh flakes, it is done.
Serve straight off the fire with the remaining glaze.
chefTips: Skin side down for most of the cook. The skin is a shield; flip it early and the flesh dries out and sticks.
Dry the fish before it goes near the fire. A wet snoek steams instead of taking on colour and glaze.
Baste only while the flesh is facing up. Basting a skin side that is against the coals just burns sugar.
Medium coals. Apricot jam is mostly sugar and it blackens fast over high heat.
The fork test is the only reliable doneness check — insert it in the thickest part and turn it slightly, and look for the flesh to flake.

Some cooks sear the flesh side first for about four minutes to set a golden colour, then turn it skin side down for the rest. It is a deliberate alternative rather than a mistake, and it gives more colour on the flesh at the cost of some moisture.
Foil under the skin makes life easier on a hot fire and lets you brown the skin properly at the end. Straight on the grid tastes better.
commonMistakes: Braaiing it flesh side down for most of the cook.
Hot coals, which burn the glaze before the fish is cooked.
Overcooking it — snoek goes from flaking to dry in about two minutes.
servedWith: Sweet potato baked in the coals
storage: Refrigerate up to 2 days. Leftovers make excellent snoekpate.
reheating: Best eaten cold the next day rather than reheated.
healthBenefits: Snoek is high in protein and omega-3 fatty acids.
Grilled over coals rather than fried.
The glaze adds sugar and butter, so this is not a lean preparation — but the fish underneath is.
culturalNote: Snoek and apricot jam is one of those pairings that looks wrong written down and is completely right on a plate. It belongs to Lambert's Bay, St Helena Bay and Paternoster, where the fish is landed, and it travelled to every braai in the Western Cape from there. The instruction to hang the fish in a draught is a small piece of honesty about who the recipe was written for.
